topic: Why does holding your breath start to burn?
title: Holding Your Breath
idea: The panic when you hold your breath is a carbon dioxide alarm; your oxygen is still around 92 percent.
hook: Why does holding your breath start to burn so fast?

beats.line: Sitting on dry land? Hold your breath with me. Ten seconds.
beats.see: Hero sits on a couch, puffs his cheeks on 'Hold'; a big 10 second countdown ring starts on 'Ten' and runs through the next three beats.

beats.line: Feel the pressure in your chest?
beats.see: Countdown at 7; a red pressure gauge on the hero's chest climbs on 'pressure', his face turns pink.

beats.line: Feels like you're out of oxygen, right?
beats.see: Countdown at 5; a paper O2 tank icon above his head starts flashing EMPTY on 'oxygen'.

beats.line: You're not. Carbon dioxide is piling up and setting off the alarm.
beats.see: Countdown at 2; the tank stops flashing and stays mostly full on 'not', CO2 bubbles stack up inside him on 'piling', an alarm bell rings on 'alarm'.
Countdown hits 0 on 'Ten'; hero exhales a big puff on 'Breathe', gauge drops back to normal.

beats.line: In one study, untrained people quit after about a minute, still near ninety two percent oxygen.
beats.see: Row of paper people gasping, a stopwatch shows ~1:00; a big oxygen meter beside them stays high and stamps 92% on 'ninety two'.

beats.line: One. Keep it short. Ten seconds is plenty.
beats.see: Step card 1 KEEP IT SHORT; the countdown ring from before shrinks to a small 10 badge on 'short'.

beats.line: Two. Never breathe fast and deep first. It hides the alarm.
beats.see: Step card 2 NO FAST BREATHING; hero panting fast, the alarm bell gets covered with a sock on 'hides'.

beats.line: Three. Never do it in water. Blackouts there come without warning.
beats.see: Step card 3 NOT IN WATER; a pool with a big red X on 'water', lights blink out with no alarm bell on 'without'.

end.line: So that burn you felt? Carbon dioxide, not missing oxygen.
end.see: Back to the hero on the couch, the CO2 bubbles light up on 'Carbon', the O2 tank shows full with a check on 'oxygen'.

description: Hold your breath with me for ten seconds. That burn is not what you think it is.

facts.claim: The urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising carbon dioxide, not by running out of oxygen.
facts.source: Pernett, Schagatay & Holmstrom, Frontiers in Physiology 2024/25 https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2024.1515232/full

facts.claim: Untrained people (81 non-divers) gave up after about 60 to 80 seconds with blood oxygen still around 92 %.
facts.source: Pernett et al., Frontiers in Physiology (same URL)

facts.claim: Hyperventilating first lowers CO2, delays the urge and raises the risk of blacking out, underwater without warning.
facts.source: DAN https://dan.org/alert-diver/article/hypoxia-in-breath-hold-diving/ ; US Naval Safety Command 'Shallow Water Blackout'

facts.claim: Safe viewer moment: 10 to 15 s sitting on dry land only; never in water, never after hyperventilating.
facts.source: FACTS file safety rule (DAN ; US Naval Safety Command)

notes: Safety: hold is 10 seconds, sitting, dry land, said in the first beat; step One explicitly caps it. 'About a minute' simplifies the study's 60 to 80 s range. 92 % is the OK-number. Records (Mifsud, Maricic) deliberately left out so nothing invites a long hold. Pacing: the 10 s countdown covers beats 1 to 5; check in the edit that the voice-over reaches 'Ten. Breathe.' at roughly 10 s after 'Hold', otherwise shorten the countdown label to match real time.
